chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibrahim al-Karkhi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I bought a female slave for Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). When I went to pay them, I said, 'Should I deduct (for defects)?' He said, 'No, indeed the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) forbade deduction after the transaction.'
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is to be understood as indicating a type of dislike (karahah), and that which reveals this is what has been narrated:

key_terms.الاستحطاط: Deducting price for defects after a transaction
key_terms.الكَرَاهِيَة: Dislike (a degree below prohibition in jurisprudence)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on deducting price for defects after completing a sale in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the post-sale deduction of price for defects (*al-istihitat*), where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) cites the Prophet’s prohibition. However, Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that this is *karahiyyah* (dislike/preference) rather than *haram* (absolute prohibition), allowing flexibility in commercial transactions. This reflects the Shia juristic principle of balancing prophetic tradition with practical commercial needs.
